# Results — Study 465 (Broadening Formation / megaphone top)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **a
broadening formation (diverging higher highs + lower lows, an expanding "megaphone" range)
marks an exhausted top that reverses down: short the break of the lower boundary** — encoded as
a mechanical rule. Pivots are confirmed fractals (k = 10, with a 10-bar confirmation lag); at
every bar we take the last two confirmed swing highs and lows, require the highs to be rising
**and** the lows falling (a diverging megaphone), and fire a **short** on the first close below
the lower boundary, entered at the **next close** (one documented lag); we measure the forward
5/10/20/60-day return of the short. Offline & deterministic once cached; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) closes for **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD** (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-05-29 (**As-of 2026-05-31**, partial June dropped; **21.4** years) |
| SPY fingerprint | `4cb5244f3990` (sha1[:12] of the close column, As-of slice) |
| Entries | **25** mechanical lower-boundary megaphone breaks pooled across the 5 tapes (k = 10) |
| Timing / costs | confirmed-fractal pivots usable only **+10 bars** later; enter the **next close** (one lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per break; returns are signed for a **short** |

> **A genuinely rare pattern.** A strict megaphone — two rising swing highs *and* two falling
> swing lows, then a lower-boundary break — fires only **25 times in 21 years across 5 indices**.
> That scarcity is honest: the believers point to a handful of textbook charts, and a handful is
> all the mechanical rule finds. The thin sample is itself part of the verdict.

## The signal — lower-break short vs a drift-matched random short baseline (the honest test)

One-sample *t* is the **misleading** number here (a short on an up-drifting index loses by
construction — negative beta); the **Welch break-vs-random** *t* is the test that matters.
Δ = short − random-short.

| horizon | n | short | win% | one-sample *t* | random short | Δ (short−random) | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 25 | −207.6 bps | 16% | −4.45 | −10.3 bps | **−197.4 bps** | −209.6 bps | −3.13 | 0.004 |
| 10-day | 25 | −172.9 bps | 32% | −3.04 | −53.6 bps | **−119.4 bps** | −174.9 bps | −1.70 | 0.099 |
| 20-day | 25 | −320.9 bps | 20% | −3.07 | −33.1 bps | **−287.9 bps** | −322.9 bps | −2.33 | 0.027 |
| 60-day | 25 | −938.7 bps | 16% | −3.73 | −118.9 bps | **−819.8 bps** | −940.7 bps | −3.91 | 0.001 |

Read it carefully. The megaphone short loses money at **every** horizon — but so does a random
short, because the tape drifts up. The decisive comparison is short-vs-random: the megaphone
short is **worse than a random short at every horizon** (Δ = −197 / −119 / −288 / −820 bps), and
the Welch *t* is **negative** (−3.13 / −1.70 / −2.33 / −3.91). Far from forecasting a turn, the
"reversal" short bleeds *more* than shorting on random days — it is short the very moments the
up-drifting index has just shaken out weak hands and resumed climbing. There is **no edge** in
either direction that survives the drift baseline; the broadening break does not forecast a top.

## Per-ticker (H = 20) — no coherent edge, and the sample is paper-thin per name

| ticker | entries | short | one-sample *t* | random short | Δ (short−random) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 7 | −416.8 bps | −3.38 | −39.3 bps | **−377.5 bps** |
| QQQ | 11 | −451.4 bps | −2.38 | −88.2 bps | **−363.2 bps** |
| IWM | 2 | +333.9 bps | n/a | −2.7 bps | **+336.6 bps** |
| DIA | 1 | −765.8 bps | n/a | −33.7 bps | **−732.0 bps** |
| GLD | 4 | −10.6 bps | n/a | −1.5 bps | **−9.1 bps** |

Four of the five names have a *single-digit* number of megaphone breaks — too few to estimate
anything. The two with a usable count (SPY, QQQ) both have the short **deeply behind** a random
short (−377, −363 bps). The lone "win" (IWM, +337 bps) rests on **two** trades. No coherent,
cross-sectional reversal edge — the hallmark of a non-signal on a tiny, noisy sample.

## Geometry placebo — scramble the megaphone, nothing changes

The decisive "does the diverging geometry matter?" test: keep the pivot **positions** and
**kinds** and the price **marginal**, but permute which price sits at which pivot, so the
rising-highs/falling-lows structure becomes meaningless. If price genuinely respected *this
specific megaphone*, the scramble would change the result.

| test | observed lower-break 20d short | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY shuffled-pivot megaphone | −416.8 bps | **0.974** | 500 |

**97% of scrambled-geometry megaphones do at least as well as the real one** (*p* = 0.974) — i.e.
the real megaphone sits at the *bad* end even of nonsense draws. The diverging-boundary geometry
carries no information; "the broadening top reverses" is busted.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real megaphone reversal

On a deterministic tape with a *planted* expanding-range reversal (knob `edge`: the channel
literally fans out and a real decline follows the lower-boundary break), the same short rule
behaves exactly as it must — so the flat/negative real-tape result is a genuine "nothing there",
not a dead detector.

| planted edge | n | short | win% | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no reversal) | 9 | −82.2 bps | 67% | −0.93 |
| **0.50** (real planted megaphone reversal) | 8 | +515.3 bps | 100% | **+6.88** |

With no planted reversal the control sits at *t* ≈ 0 (no false positive); a real planted
expanding-range reversal lights up at *t* = +6.88 with a 100% win-rate (the short banks the
decline). The detector is live — so the real-tape result is an honest null.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The megaphone-break short does **not** beat a drift-matched random short —
  it is *worse* at every horizon (Δ = −197 / −119 / −288 / −820 bps at 5/10/20/60 days; Welch
  *t* = −3.13 / −1.70 / −2.33 / −3.91). The negative one-sample *t*'s are pure negative beta
  (a short on an up-drifting index), not a reversal edge. Only **25** breaks in 21 years.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** There is nothing to deploy: long or short, the broadening break has
  no residual edge once the index's drift is accounted for, the per-name sample is paper-thin,
  and costs only deepen the hole. Fading or following the megaphone are equally pointless.
- **"Does expanding volatility forecast a turn?" — BUSTED.** The shuffled-pivot placebo leaves
  the result intact (*p* = 0.974): scrambled-geometry megaphones do as well as the real one, so
  the diverging-boundary structure carries no forecasting information. Expanding range marks no
  turn; the megaphone is a descriptive pattern, not a forecast.
